prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Link Inventory Audit — Q1 2025 (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Page title" · longest unbreakable word 88px · one-line width 282px
  col 2: header "URL" · longest unbreakable word 287px · one-line width 744px
  col 3: header "Last checked" · longest unbreakable word 54px · one-line width 84px
  col 4: header "Status code" · longest unbreakable word 42px · one-line width 76px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 767px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 766px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 767px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Audit a set of links by identifying each page and URL alongside its most recent check and resulting status code.","reading":"Readers scan page titles to find an entry, follow the row to its URL, and compare check dates and status codes across entries. Wrapped titles and URLs can share the same row height, provided each row remains easy to follow.","groups":["Page title and URL identify the same destination; the title supports scanning while the URL gives the precise address.","Last checked and Status code describe the result of the audit and should remain compact and easy to compare vertically."],"keep_intact":["Dates and status codes","Unbreakable URL segments","Individual words in page titles and column headers"],"may_wrap":["Page titles at natural word boundaries","URLs at available break opportunities"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[160,404,105,97],"idea":"Prioritize URL readability, allowing longer page titles to wrap into the height already needed by long addresses."},{"name":"B","widths":[220,344,105,97],"idea":"Balance title scanning and URL space while keeping the audit columns compact."},{"name":"C","widths":[253,311,105,97],"idea":"Favor quick recognition of page titles while giving the URL column enough room for its longest unbreakable segment."}]}
